name: Cartridge razor
lead: A cartridge razor is a manual razor whose blades, typically two to six or more, are mounted in a disposable plastic cartridge that clips onto a reusable handle. Men and women use it to remove facial or body hair, and for facial shaving the point is a clean-shaven, neat jawline and cheeks that many people feel looks sharper and more groomed; the multiple blades and a lubricating strip are designed to give a close shave with little skill.[1][2]

The design was introduced commercially in 1970 by Wilkinson, whose Bonded Shaving System embedded a single blade in a disposable cartridge, and Gillette answered in 1971 with the twin-blade Trac II.[1] Cartridge and disposable razors have been the predominant type of razor since the 1970s, and manufacturers have since added blades, with market commentary and Wikipedia noting that multi-blade cartridges carry high profit margins and tie buyers to proprietary cartridges.[1]

Researchers have compared razor designs on skin redness. A 2024 study in 59 men compared a cartridge razor with a safety razor and found more shaving-induced redness with the cartridge.[3] Wikipedia notes that multi-blade razors cut very close and that some people prone to razor bumps switch to single- or double-blade razors or to electric shavers.[2] Skin appearance after shaving therefore depends on both razor design and technique.

paras: A cartridge head carries a row of fixed blades, often with a lubricating strip typically made of polyethylene glycol that helps them glide, and the cartridge is replaced when the blades dull.[2] Cartridge razors are one of several wet-shaving options alongside straight razors, double-edge safety razors, single-edge and injector razors and disposables; electric shavers use oscillating or rotating blades behind a perforated screen and cause fewer cuts, though they may not shave as closely.[2]

Wikipedia's shaving article describes technique points that apply to cartridge shaving: softening hair with warm water first, using a lubricant such as cream, soap or gel, shaving with the grain, using a fresh blade, applying light pressure, and making several passes rather than removing all stubble at once.[2] Aftershaves may contain antiseptic alcohol, fragrance or moisturizers, and gentle exfoliation before and after shaving is described as reducing ingrown hairs and snagging.[2]

Wikipedia also notes that shaving does not make hair grow back thicker, coarser or darker; the blunt tip of cut hair makes it feel that way.[2] Men's forum threads on T Nation discuss the cost of proprietary cartridges against wet shaving with a double-edge razor,[4] and whether electric or traditional razors suit better.[5]

Wilkinson's 1970 system placed one blade in a disposable cartridge. Gillette's 1971 Trac II used two blades, and Gillette claimed the pair gave a closer shave through a hysteresis effect, a claim whose practical importance Wikipedia says has been questioned.[1] Bic launched the fully disposable razor in 1974, and Gillette's Good News followed in the US in 1976.[1]

The three-blade Mach3 appeared in 1998, after which Gillette's blade sales are reported to have risen 50 percent; Schick responded with the four-blade Quattro. A five-blade Gillette razor reached the market in 2006, and Dorco released six- and later seven-blade cartridges starting in 2012.[1] Gillette's vibrating Fusion Power and M3Power models were the subject of a US court ruling that their vibration claims were unsubstantiated and inaccurate.[1]

Shaving can cause cuts, abrasions and irritation. Razor burn, a mild rash that usually fades within hours to days, is typically linked to dry shaving, blunt blades, heavy pressure or shaving against the grain, and razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae) are persistent inflammation that can appear as red welts or pustules in severe cases.[2] The 2024 erythema study identifies shaving-induced redness as a quantifiable outcome of razor choice.[3]

A 2024 study used multispectral near-infrared spectroscopy imaging to measure shaving-induced erythema in 59 healthy men, shaving one side of the face or neck with a safety razor and the other with a three-blade cartridge razor.[2] Skin oxygen saturation measurements showed significantly less erythema with the safety razor: immediately after shaving, 40.3 percent of safety-razor skin was affected versus 57.6 percent for the cartridge razor, and 36.5 versus 53.8 percent at five minutes.[2] The study compared a single safety-razor and a single cartridge design, so its findings apply to those products.

card.summary: The standard multi-blade razor with a disposable head; one 59-man study found it left more redness than a safety razor.
card.note: Single comparison study (cartridge vs safety razor); proprietary cartridges tie buyers to a brand.

quick.overview:
A cartridge razor clips a disposable multi-blade head onto a handle. It has been the dominant style of razor since the 1970s, and makers have steadily added more blades.

It is a grooming tool with no lasting effect on appearance. The main published comparison found more redness than with a safety razor.
quick.mechanism: Several blades set in a row in the cartridge cut the hair in successive passes; the cartridge snaps off when dull.
quick.risks: Razor-related redness and irritation were higher with a three-blade cartridge than a safety razor in one 2024 study of 59 men. Cuts are possible with any razor.

angle.text: A cartridge razor removes facial hair quickly and closely, giving a clean-shaven look with a visible jawline. Post-shave redness and bumps in some users are part of how people choose between razor types.
